about.title: Who we are
about.p1: We are a team of drama educators who, since 2016, have been designing and delivering the Mikroi Ichneytes educational programme as part of the Athens Epidaurus Festival. We facilitate drama education programmes for children aged 5–10, drawing inspiration from ancient drama and contemporary stage interpretations of myth. Our experience at Epidaurus forms the foundation of our work and serves as a starting point for exploring new ways of engaging with ancient drama, with the aim of nurturing the theatre audiences of tomorrow through our work with children.
about.p2: Our interests span a wide range of theatrical texts and genres: from ancient drama and theatrical mythologies to contemporary dramaturgy and new forms of stage storytelling. We explore the questions, conflicts, and human experiences conveyed by these works, examining how they resonate with the world we live in today. With Educational Drama at the heart of our approach, and drawing on our experience in drama education, we create a space where children and adults can engage with theatre through direct experience, interpret it, and build their own bridges between myth and their everyday lives.

do.title: Discover what we do
do.quote: “Here, nothing is imitation. Everything is about creating and playing.”
do.intro: We design a “journey”: the children follow the traces of a story we create and, through a series of activities, are gradually immersed in a multimodal world that unfolds and takes shape along the way.

thefirsttrace.title: The First Trace
thefirsttrace.text: A story often begins with a trace: an object appears as if by magic, out of place in its surroundings, and everyone wonders how it got there and what it might mean. They follow the trail step by step, like trackers, and a mystery gradually unfolds: a place, a memory, a name pieced together syllable by syllable. This trace moves freely through time. It might be something entirely modern, even futuristic, or a fragment of another story that suddenly casts our own in a different light.

thresholdsandtransitions.title: Thresholds and Transitions
thresholdsandtransitions.text: To enter the dramatic world of the programme, the children pass through symbolic thresholds and make step-by-step transitions that lead them ever deeper into the world of myth. An artistic object 'unlocks' the story for them. They step between the reeds blocking the entrance to a temple, purify their hands by following a ritual, pass through a circular gateway, knock on a door, and are greeted by a character from the drama.

materialsreimagined.title: Materials Reimagined
materialsreimagined.text: In Mikroi Ichneytes, a cardboard box becomes the walls of Troy, a plastic bottle conceals a message from Orestes asking for help, and a pebble becomes the pendant by which Electra recognises her brother. The children transform everyday, natural, or recyclable materials into elements of a world that takes shape with their participation. They often create large, collaborative constructions whose purpose is only revealed later: what they have made with their own hands becomes part of the action and of the world we explore together.

thefacilitatorperformer.title: The Facilitator Performer
thefacilitatorperformer.text: The Mikroi Ichneytes have no time for authority figures. We prefer to get confused, make mistakes, and ask the children for help. Their ideas can change the course of our shared adventure. As actors, we remain alert, truly listen to our fellow players, and respond in the moment. A child once called us 'actors-teachers': when we play alongside the children, she explained, we understand them better. This is how the facilitator-performer emerges: a fellow traveller and playmate at every step of the story.

collectiveroles.title: Collective Roles
collectiveroles.text: In Mikroi Ichneytes, the children enter the story as a community with a mission. They become worshippers at a temple, inhabitants of a city, followers of a hero, or costume designers for a performance. They encounter dilemmas, share ideas, disagree, and decide how to act. Every child brings their own voice to our shared world. By stepping into the lives of others, we discover together new ways of seeing our own...

theroleofexpert.title: The Role of the Expert
theroleofexpert.text: A more specialised form of collective role: the children informally take on a professional identity, such as archaeological site conservators or museum curators, and behave as though they already know what they are only just discovering. Without realising it, they 'know' far more than they think. As experts, they are called upon to investigate information, solve riddles, and piece together clues, until the entire world of myth unfolds before them, along with the issue on which they must take a stand.

mapping.title: Mapping
mapping.text: 'At the roundabout, take the last exit towards Perdition Street... Continue until you reach the black lake with the ferryman. Pay him no attention. He takes far too long. Go straight past him!' Audio GPS guides, curious directions, maps, signs, and imaginary streets create a landscape of wandering and exploration that extends into the surrounding environment, connecting it with the dramatic world of the programme.

multimodalenvironments.title: Multimodal Environments
multimodalenvironments.text: Light, shadow, projections, moving images, and sound come together to create a multimodal universe: animal shadows, star-filled skies, and shifting colours bring to life stories that cannot be conveyed through realistic stage representation. The boundaries between storytelling, imagery, and space become fluid, and the imaginary world itself becomes part of the action. The children move through and explore this world as though they inhabit it, if only for a little while.

throughthepuppet.title: Through the Puppet
throughthepuppet.text: The puppet becomes an independent dramatic character, giving voice to figures experiencing intense emotions, difficult situations, or moral dilemmas. Its small scale and physical presence create a safe bridge between the children and the character, allowing them to approach fear, loss, guilt, or suffering from a distance and in safety. Sometimes the puppeteer also appears in character alongside the puppet: two dramatic figures sharing the stage. Depending on the needs of the story, the relationship between the puppet, the puppeteer, and the children takes on a different form each time.

shadowtheatre.title: Shadow Theatre
shadowtheatre.text: Light and shadow transform the body: a facilitator becomes a shadow within a palace, a divine figure, or a Fate who determines a hero's destiny. Behind the screen, scale can shift freely, allowing difficult or emotionally charged moments, such as conflict or loss, to become the subject of poetic storytelling, like a fairy tale. The power of shadow lies in its simplicity and abstraction, leaving an empty space for the children's imagination to fill.

contemporarycontexts.title: Contemporary Contexts
contemporarycontexts.text: An issue explored in a tragic text often finds its resonance in the present day. How can children grasp the meaning of supplication? Betrayal? Power? The Mikroi Ichneytes travel in time machines and often encounter contemporary forms of vulnerability along the way: a Roma child selling flowers, a skeleton who deals in weapons in a war zone, a woman who dares to defy social conventions and combs her hair in the light. In this way, an ancient dilemma takes on a contemporary human face.

allegories.title: Allegories
allegories.text: When a story ventures into dark and violent territory, the myth is often reconstructed through an entirely new system of imagery that preserves its intensity without realistically depicting violence. In the Oresteia, for example, a lion, a lioness, a wolf, and a nightingale took on the roles of the protagonists, drawn from the very metaphors Aeschylus uses to describe his characters: the net that traps the lion becomes the means by which Agamemnon is led to his death. The children follow the story, gradually connecting the animals with the characters and the relationships between them.

festival.findUs: Find us at the Athens Epidaurus Festival

1.text: When I came to pick him up, he said, “Mom, why did you come so quickly? I wanted to be the last to leave!” He kept talking about the experience the next morning too. You created a beautiful link between the experiences of parents and children.

2.text: They discovered the myth of Iphigenia in an interactive way and were gently introduced to ancient theatre. Later, as we discussed the performance and they shared their activity, it felt as though we had all experienced the same story.

3.text: We still talk about The Birds and what they would like to change before returning to the city. From The Bacchae, they remember the gods, while the masks and Dionysian wreaths they made still decorate their desks.

4.text: She happily described the crafts, the gold, the museum, and the conflict between Wealth and Poverty. The children found their own solution through solidarity, cooperation and sharing: “Wealth is family and time spent with friends.”

5.text: It is not just a place where I feel safe leaving the children during the performance. They genuinely look forward to it, leave having learned something, and afterwards we can all talk about what they experienced and what we saw.

6.text: The children talked about the symbols in the performance, the large dog they built from boxes, and the theatre itself. Afterwards, we could discuss it all together: me as a spectator, and the children through their own experience in the programme.

7.text: After the performance and over the following days, all three children shared, each in their own way and with great excitement, details from the activities. We talked a lot about the play and about how each of them understood the idea of Wealth.

8.text: It was a new and wonderful experience for all three of them. They gained meaningful knowledge about the play and the Theatre of Epidaurus and, with the educators’ guidance, worked beautifully together and stayed happily throughout the workshop.

9.text: Being able to watch the performance knowing that your child is creatively engaged in a welcoming environment, and then being able to share your experiences around the same theme afterwards, is incredibly valuable.

10.text: For a child to stay in the space for three hours, be completely happy, never complain, and actually look forward to going back is amazing to me. The work being done here is truly exceptional!

11.text: Uh, I think that you are actors - teachers because actors - teachers are usually kinder than normal ones. [Nina, 8]

12.text: She wanted to listen to Maria Callas. She told us that when Callas sang, she was free.

13.text: The spontaneous use of the verb 'we were' to describe the roles in the scenes dramatised by the Mikroi Ichneytes (e.g. 'We were soldiers'). There was a clear sense of togetherness and of the story coming to life.

14.text: The opportunity to engage in creative activities as a group in a place so rich in artistic significance and marked by modern history. An immersive experience in nature, inspired by great works that explore human instincts and weaknesses! An encounter with life as portrayed through art!

15.text: The fact that a six-year-old child has the unique opportunity, at such a young age, to visit such an important UNESCO World Heritage site, not simply as a visitor but as an active participant in a programme connected to the site's use from antiquity to the present day, is an extraordinary benefit and a strong motivation for us to take part in activities of this kind.

16.text: 'Mum, today I lived a dream!! Can you please take me there again?'
